articles.title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop. Hundreds of O'Hare, Midway flights remain delayed or canceled
articles.text:
FAA lifts nationwide ground stop. Hundreds of O'Hare, Midway flights remain delayed or canceled - WBEZ Chicago
Passengers wait in line to speak with a United Airlines agent after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop at O’Hare Airport.
Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times
Transportation
Travel
Nation/World
FAA lifts nationwide ground stop. Hundreds of O'Hare, Midway flights remain delayed or canceled
The Federal Aviation Administration ordered all departing traffic to be grounded Friday afternoon due to a nationwide issue with traffic control communication. Hundreds of flights at Midway and O’Hare airports were affected for several hours even after the ground stop was lifted.
By
Mariah Rush,  David Struett and  Violet Miller
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Hours after the Federal Aviation Administration halted all flights across the country Friday, causing widespread delays and cancellations at O’Hare and Midway airports, the agency said departures could resume.
Officials blamed “an incredibly old air traffic control system” for instability in air traffic control communications during a White House briefing Friday evening.
Inside O’Hare International Airport — the busiest airport in the U.S. — confused passengers wandered around as luggage piled up on baggage carousels. Long lines of travelers rummaged through hundreds of bags from flights that never took off because of the delay.
The FAA had grounded all flights nationwide at around 2:36 p.m., and an FAA alert said the stoppage was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
At the time, 3,500 airplanes were in the air, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.
The order was lifted at 7:15 p.m., though it was unclear when flights actually would resume.
A sudden silence fell over O’Hare as travelers were notified that the ground stop had been lifted. But a video board displaying flight information still showed delays or cancellations even though many passengers attempted to buy tickets at nearby airline kiosks.
“For an 18-hour trip back and forth, it doesn’t make sense for us and try to go,” said Angelica Colmenares, who was en route to Paris for a 48-hour trip with a friend. Luckily, we were flying standby so we didn’t fly, but now we’re going to have our own party in Chicago.”
An hour after the ground stoppage was lifted, American Airlines said it was “prioritizing flights to non-hub cities, as well as international flying, to position aircraft and crew where they are needed to help restore our operation.”
“We expect residual delays and cancellations tonight and into tomorrow following the FAA’s nationwide ground stop,” the statement said.
Travelers flying to, t hrough, or from select airports on Friday and Saturday — including O’Hare— are eligible for a waived change fee, but changes must be booked by Saturday, according to American Airlines.
United Airlines and Southwest Airlines also offered refunds or changes to flights for free. Chicago-based United noted the reschedule deadline for travel on Friday and Saturday would be Nov. 20.
Southwest offered customers that were traveling on Friday through Monday, Nov. 16 the option to either keep the reservation, rebook within five days of the original travel date or to request a refund. Refunds are eligible for passengers whose flights were canceled or “significantly delayed.”
Southwest also noted that while flights had resumed, “customers may continue to experience delays and cancellations.”
But most of the flights scheduled through Friday night — all through Southwest — were canceled at Midway.
“We’ve opened up the airspace,” Duffy said. “Now does that mean every flight is going to fly right now? It’s going to be slow, right? So if you’re watching, and you’re at an airport, check with your airline. It depends on do we have crews available, do we have pilots and flight attendants available to fly your flight?”
At O’Hare, many were also canceled, but more were still estimated to depart after long delays.
Some airlines, including JetBlue and Air Canada, had already said they were canceling the rest of their Friday night flights.
U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the public was “never in danger” and the flights were grounded due to an “abundance of caution.”
By 5:30 p.m., O’Hare had reported 328 flight cancellations and 847 delays. Midway saw 30 canceled flights and 186 delays, according to the Chicago Department of Aviation. At 6:15 p.m., 30 flights scheduled to arrive at O’Hare since 2:55 p.m. had been diverted. Ten arrivals scheduled at Midway were also diverted.
By 10 p.m., O’Hare’s number of cancellations had reached 889, and delays hit 990. Midway had 61 canceled and195 delayed.
Duffy said an overload in the FAA’s analog telecommunications led to instability that affected all of the nation’s 22 air traffic control centers that route planes between airports.
During the evening briefing, Duffy shifted focus to a political fight, saying the Trump administration had been “asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system.”
"[The aircrafts flying] landed... But you will have more of these. You will have more of them unless the American people and Congress tell us to build,” he said.
Mullin said there was no sign that “this was a nefarious attack against us. It’s just a telecommunications outage.”
Although the order was lifted, Duffy said he expected it to take a bit to catch up on flight schedules. “Hopefully (Saturday), we are going to start to see far better movement,” he said.
Earlier at O’Hare, video boards displaying flight information were checkered with red and yellow, signifying the delays and cancellations that forced many travelers to book hotel rooms for the night or rent a car to arrive at their destinations.

articles.title: The Rundown: Another sudden Johnson administration departure
articles.text:
The Rundown: Another sudden Johnson administration departure - WBEZ Chicago
Mayor Brandon Johnson on Oct. 21, 2026.
Ashlee Rezin/Chicago Sun-Times
The Rundown: WBEZ’s Daily Newsletter
The Rundown: Another sudden Johnson administration departure
Plus, Evanston musician Jason Narducy’s rock ‘n’ roll tales. Here’s what you need to know today.
By
Bianca Cseke
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Good afternoon! It’s Friday the 13th, and my black cat is displeased he didn’t get an extra-early breakfast to celebrate. Here’s what you need to know today.
1. Mayor Johnson’s chief financial officer abruptly resigned, becoming the third CFO to quit in a year
As Fran Spielman reports for the Chicago Sun-Times, Ashlee Gabrysch’s departure sent shock waves through City Hall and beyond, coming in the middle of a budget stalemate after just three months in the role. The move could trigger another drop in Chicago’s already shaky bond rating and scare investors away from the city’s bonds.
A former Wall Street executive, Gabrysch issued a statement saying she was unwilling to compromise her financial integrity. She did not reveal what she was asked to do that would have damaged her reputation.
“As the City of Chicago’s Chief Financial Officer, there is nothing more important than my fiduciary duty to the City and its taxpayers. The Chief Financial Officer’s statements about city finances are not idle chatter: they are relied upon by investors, ratings agencies, City Council, and taxpayers. The CFO must act scrupulously to ensure they are always accurate and complete,” Gabrysch said in a statement.
“Throughout my career, I have remained committed to upholding the highest standards of financial integrity and transparency, and in my short time as Chief Financial Officer, I have faithfully discharged this duty. It has become apparent, however, that to continue in this role would be to compromise my integrity and professional obligations. I therefore have concluded that I must step down from my role, and hereby tender my resignation.”
Gabrysch had replaced Steven Mahr, who himself had abruptly resigned, along with his top deputy. Mahr had replaced Jill Jaworski, who left City Hall in January for a job at Navy Pier shortly after a City Council majority rejected Johnson’s corporate head tax and muscled through an alternative city budget. [ Chicago Sun-Times]
2. Why is Chicago alderperson a job few want? In February, 11 ward races will be uncontested
The Chicago City Council is more independent than ever, forcing Mayor Brandon Johnson to issue four vetoes, cast three tie-breaking votes, accept a Zoning Committee chair he did not choose and struggle to pass two budgets with mounting resistance for a third.
Despite the transition to more power, 10 incumbents and one newcomer won’t have to raise a penny or spend a minute shaking hands, knocking on doors or attending neighborhood forums ahead of the city’s Feb. 23 aldermanic election, my colleague Fran Spielman reports.
The incumbents are Alds. Lamont Robinson (4th), Peter Chico (10th), Nicole Lee (11th), Ray Lopez (15th), Ronnie Mosley (21st), Samantha Nugent (39th), Andre Vasquez (40th), Anthony Napolitano (41st), Matt Martin (47th) and Debra Silverstein (50th). Meanwhile, Elianne Bahena is chief of staff to — and handpicked successor of — retiring Ald. Michael Rodriguez (22nd).
Other veterans will likely face only nominal opposition from challengers with very little money: Brian Hopkins (2nd); Pat Dowell (3rd); Desmon Yancy (5th); Monique Scott (24th); Felix Cardona (31st); Bill Conway (34th); Gilbert Villegas (36th); Nick Sposato (38th); Brendan Reilly (42nd); Timmy Knudsen (43rd) and Bennett Lawson (44th).
“It’s possible that our constituents are pleased to see a City Council with teeth and a coalition of aldermen who are stepping up, doing the hard work and pushing back on the executive branch of government for the first time in many, many decades,” said Reilly, a leader of the group that calls itself the Common Sense Caucus. “In other cases, maybe it’s a job they simply don’t want. There’s so much upheaval at City Hall, perhaps some folks don’t want to sign up for that circus.” [ Chicago Sun-Times]
3. Lurie Children’s received state approval for a $480 million hospital in Downers Grove
This funding paves the way for the health system’s first inpatient hospital outside its Chicago campus, Misha Manjuran Oberoi reports for the Chicago Sun-Times.
The Illinois Health Facilities and Services Review Board approved the hospital’s Certificate of Need application, a key step toward expanding pediatric emergency and specialty care in the western suburbs.
“Every child deserves access to the specialized care they need, as close to home as possible,” Tom Shanley, the hospital’s president and CEO, said in a statement.
The proposed 298,000-square-foot facility will include 48 inpatient beds, an emergency department, operating rooms, diagnostic imaging and outpatient services. It is also expected to offer specialties in oncology, cardiology, gastroenterology and orthopedics. Patients are expected to begin receiving care in spring 2029. [ Chicago Sun-Times]
4. Chicago’s Thanksgiving Parade will start an hour earlier for the first time
For the first time in its 92-year history, the Thanksgiving Day procession will begin at 7:45 a.m. — an hour earlier than in previous years, according to a spokesperson for the parade’s organizers.
The earlier start will allow the parade’s television broadcast to begin at 8 a.m. on CBS Chicago, ahead of the Bears’ Thanksgiving Day game against the Detroit Lions. Pregame coverage will follow at 10 a.m.
The parade along State Street will start at Ida B. Wells Drive and head north to Randolph Street. Admission is free. Expect to see 14 giant balloons, 12 marching bands and six equestrian units, with a new Cookie Monster balloon among the attractions. [ Chicago Sun-Times]

articles.text:
Mayor Johnson's chief financial officer abruptly resigns, third CFO to quit in a year - WBEZ Chicago

City of Chicago via LinkedIn
City Hall

Mayor Johnson's chief financial officer abruptly resigns, third CFO to quit in a year
In her resignation letter, Ashlee Gabrysch said she felt compelled to quit because “to continue in this role would be to compromise my integrity and professional obligations.”
By
Fran Spielman
Updated
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
The abrupt resignation Friday of Mayor Brandon Johnson’s third chief financial officer in a year could trigger another drop in Chicago’s bond rating — and the events that led to her departure cast a damning, harsh light on Johnson’s leadership as he seeks a second term.
Ashlee Gabrysch’s departure sent shock waves through City Hall and beyond. Her resignation comes in the middle of a budget stalemate and after just three months as the city’s top financial officer. Even more damaging than Gabrysch’s sudden exit is what she said on her way out the door.
A former Wall Street executive, Gabrysch issued a statement saying she was unwilling to compromise her financial integrity.
“As the City of Chicago’s Chief Financial Officer, there is nothing more important than my fiduciary duty to the City and its taxpayers. The Chief Financial Officer’s statements about city finances are not idle chatter: they are relied upon by investors, ratings agencies, City Council, and taxpayers. The CFO must act scrupulously to ensure they are always accurate and complete,” Gabrysch said in a statement released to the media.
“Throughout my career, I have remained committed to upholding the highest standards of financial integrity and transparency, and in my short time as Chief Financial Officer, I have faithfully discharged this duty. It has become apparent, however, that to continue in this role would be to compromise my integrity and professional obligations. I therefore have concluded that I must step down from my role, and hereby tender my resignation.”
A former senior director at Fitch Ratings, Gabrysch was hired in early August to replace Steven Mahr, who abruptly resigned, along with his top deputy, just days before veteran Budget Director Annette Guzman followed both men out the door.
Mahr had replaced Jill Jaworski, who left City Hall in January for a job at Navy Pier shortly after a City Council majority rejected Johnson’s corporate head tax and muscled through an alternative city budget.
Former Chicago Chief Financial Officer Jill Jaworski in 2024
Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times
The hiring of Gabrysch sent a signal of reassurance to Wall Street, especially since Gabrysch had served as Fitch’s lead analyst for both Chicago and Illinois. That made her familiar with the city’s $36 billion pension crisis and the city’s marathon budget battle.
Civic Federation President Joe Ferguson said the resignation of Johnson’s third CFO is “spectacular, breathtaking and disturbing.”
“Credit to her for holding a line that has been fuzzy at best during this administration and doing one of the most important things that a senior-level person in that position can do, which is to say no when something crosses the line,” Ferguson said. “We don’t know what that line is. We don’t know what she has been asked to say that caused her to draw that line.”
Ferguson urged the City Council to call a hearing, summon Gabrysch to testify and find out what exactly she found so “unacceptable.”
Ald. Bill Conway (34th), a former investment banker who teaches college finance, demanded an “immediate and robust investigation.” Conway called Gabrysch’s resignation letter an “obvious indication that she was asked by the mayor’s office to present false information.”
The mayor’s office turned the tables on Gabrysch — essentially accusing her of wrongdoing serious enough to warrant an internal investigation.
“The City of Chicago is facing a serious budget crisis following decades of mismanagement. It is concerning that, during her short tenure, Ashlee was largely absent during critical periods of the City’s budget preparation process,” the statement said. “Additionally, her decision to direct the City Treasurer to issue a $75 million payment without proper legal authority or following the required processes raises serious concerns.
Mayor Brandon Johnson presents his 2027 budget during a City Council meeting earlier this fall.
Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times
“Our administration made multiple attempts to meet with her to discuss this action and seek an explanation, including shortly before her public resignation. Those attempts went unresolved. Given the seriousness of these concerns, we will refer the matter to the city’s Office of Inspector General for independent review. We welcome a full review of the conduct at issue.”
Gabrysch issued a statement in response to the mayor’s office’s remarks: “This effort by the administration to deflect from the serious issues at stake and attack those who attempt to hold them accountable is disappointing but not surprising. I stand by my statement and will continue to operate in accordance with my values and integrity.”
On opening day of City Council budget hearings, Gabrysch made a statement that signaled the trouble ahead. She contradicted Johnson’s claim that his $17.6 billion preelection budget was 76% structurally balanced.
Gabrysch said only 56% of the moves the mayor had made to erase a $882 million shortfall were structural, because settlements tied to allegations of police abuse — and the $480 million in borrowing that Johnson ordered to cover those costs — should not count as structural solutions.
“There was a collective gasp in the City Council chamber because no CFO has ever said, ‘Here’s the truth,’ ” said 32nd Ward Ald. Scott Waguespack, the former Finan

articles.title: Evanston musician Jason Narducy is back with more tales of rock ’n’ roll in ‘Mostly the Van’ part two
articles.text:
Evanston musician Jason Narducy is back with more tales of rock ’n’ roll in ‘Mostly the Van’ part two - WBEZ Chicago
Jason Narducy
Nathan Keay
Music
Arts & Culture
Evanston musician Jason Narducy is back with more tales of rock ’n’ roll in ‘Mostly the Van’ part two
There are “Behind the Music” sagas from touring with Bob Mould, Superchunk and the R.E.M. covers project with Michael Shannon. But the stories he chooses to share in glorious detail in the second volume of his memoir series are a bit more innocuous.
By
Selena Fragassi
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Jason Narducy would be the first to tell you that rock ’n’ roll stories are not all biting the heads off bats, snorting human ashes, setting hotel rooms on fire and having some intern pick out all the brown M&Ms in your dressing room.
Sure, the Evanston-reared musician has his “Behind the Music” sagas from touring with Bob Mould, Superchunk and the R.E.M. covers project with Michael Shannon. There’s also his own musical projects Split Single, Verböten and Verbow. But the tales he chooses to share in glorious detail in the second volume of his memoir series “Mostly the Van” (out Nov. 17) are a bit more innocuous. Like, getting Facebook friend requests from George Wendt, sparring with Guided By Voices’ Bob Pollard over Miller Lite vs. Heineken and playing with his band Split Single at the infamous Pizzagate restaurant in Washington, D.C., around the time the 4chan conspiracy went viral in 2016.
And there is one unbelievable story about the time he was in Paris with the band Telekinesis and, fresh from a dire tourist trip to the underground catacombs, he witnessed a motorcyclist catch on fire.
Jason Narducy Book Release Show
When: 6:30 p.m., Nov. 15
Where: SPACE, 1245 Chicago Ave., Evanston
Tickets: $20-30
Info: evanstonspace.com
Still, Narducy said, “I think most people in the general public think that if you are in the music industry, you’re either famous or you’re a hobbyist, when actually there are tens of thousands of us in here that make a living at music. Those are the stories that interest me the most. … I wanted a human thread.”
The tone is set straight away with the book title. It references a time in 2023 when Narducy was on the road again with fellow musician Kieran McCabe, and as they set foot in a Midwestern coffee shop, the barista immediately knew they were in a band. But not by reading cues of their thrifted duds or sniffing out their rock star je ne sais quoi. No, it was “mostly the van,” as she told them, referencing their beat-up sprinter outside the café windows. Plenty more humble brags ensue in the book.
With such a long touring pedigree, Narducy has plenty of stories, which made it easy to fill a second volume, nearly a year after the first was released last December. Both are on the indie imprint Porchlight Books and edited by former musician turned publishing pro, Freda Love Smith (once of alt rock group Blake Babies), who helps give the book its sharp insider edge. Photos including self-captured Polaroids, some very early iPhone snaps and the work of professionals also fill the pages. That includes two happenstance shoots with a random van outside photographer Nathan Keay’s North Side house that helped capture the essence of the book title. (Narducy donated his trusty set of wheels, Old Bessie, years ago.)
“When I was driving to [Nathan’s] house for another photo shoot, the van was still there — a year later,” Narducy said, dumbfounded. “I want to leave a note for that guy or that gal and just say, ‘Thank you. [Your van] is in a bunch of books.’”
“I think most people in the general public think that if you are in the music industry, you’re either famous or you’re a hobbyist, when actually there are tens of thousands of us in here that make a living at music. Those are the stories that interest me the most. … I wanted a human thread,” Narducy said of the latest volume in his memoir series.
Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times
But it was going back to his teenage days, around the time when the North Shore teenage punks Verböten were making waves, that sets Narducy’s latest collection apart. In the pages, there are modern-day run-ins with Dave Grohl and his mom Virginia (“Ginny” as Narducy calls her), referencing how the Foo Fighters frontman grew up with Verböten singer Tracey Bradford and credits the young group for inspiring him to write songs.
The book also starts with 19-year-old Narducy getting a call at his day job at Record Exchange on Belmont Avenue and finding out he was going to be a father. It ends with his first-born daughter, Alexa (then 8), brushing off Narducy’s “very challenging” gig singing the national anthem at a Bulls game in 2000. “I think almost every parent can relate to having a kid who just does not care about anything they do,” the musician jokes.
But the crown jewel of adolescent tales in the book, without giving too much away, involves Narducy getting yelled at by late sportscaster Tim Weigel (the stepdad of one of his high school friends) for playing music too loud and then getting caught in the crosshairs with Evanston PD for some illicit activity in Dawes Park.
“I was like, this is the first time I’m submitting a story that’s not music related. But [Freda] said, ‘I don’t know, you going toe to toe with the Evanston Police Department at age 17 is pretty rock ’n’ roll,’” Narducy said with a laugh. “It taps into that kind of teenage rebellion, a rare moment where … the cops were f------ with us, and we won.”
Guitarist Jason Narducy performs with Verboten on day two of Riot Fest in 2024, when the band reunited.
Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times file
A grown-up Verböten famously reunited in 2024 with gigs at Riot Fest as well as Metro and Salt Shed, respectively opening for Frank Black and Iggy Pop. There are no plans at this point for the group to keep going.

Where to ice skate in Chicago and the suburbs 2026 - WBEZ Chicago
Opening on Nov. 13, the Ribbon at Maggie Daley Park is one of the Loop’s most popular winter attractions.
Santiago Covarrubias / For The Sun-Times
Things to Do

Where to ice skate in Chicago and the suburbs 2026
Romantic settings under the stars, themed skate nights and Jamaican food await you at these 14 Chicago-area rinks.
By
Dorothy Hernandez
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]

With the season’s first snowflakes potentially falling on Friday, it’s a sign that now is the time to hit the rink.
Whether you have your sights set on Olympic glory or don’t know a snowplow from a salchow, one of these 14 Chicago-area venues, from great date night spots to large, regulation-sized rinks, offer something for skaters of all levels. At Skatium Ice Arena in Skokie, you’ll even find classic rink fare like burgers and nachos with Jamaican flair.
Several rinks in our list offer free admission if you bring your own skates; all of them rent skates for kids through adults. Hours of operation vary widely, and reservations are required by a few rinks. Classes for figure skating and hockey are on tap at many.
Here’s where to lace up your skates in the Chicago area this season.
Blackhawks Ice Center
1801 W. Jackson Blvd.; 312-455-7600
$12 admission; $6 skate rental
Year-round
You don’t need to be an avid Blackhawks fan to enjoy the year-round facility where the team practices. Located on the Near West Side, the Blackhawks Community Ice Rink offers regular public skates, freestyle skating drop-ins for the more advanced (you might even spot figure skater Jason Brown practicing his routines as the Olympian has recently relocated back to Chicago after training in Toronto for several years) and hockey programs for kids and adults. If you are a Blackhawks fan, practices are also open to the public; check the schedule to line up your viewing in the same excursion. Reservations or presale tickets for public skate sessions are not required but all admissions will be on a first-come, first-served basis.
Chicago Wolves Ice Rink
5501 Park Place, Rosemont; 847-349-5009
Admission free; $8 skate rental
Nov. 29-Jan. 31, 2027
The Chicago Wolves Ice Rink returns to the 200,000-square-foot Parkway Bank Park entertainment complex, giving shoppers and skaters the chance to cross off both pursuits in one trip. Once you’ve finished showing off your layback spin and Axel jump (or just safely made your way around once or twice the rink without faceplanting), transition to dinner or catch a new release at the AMC Rosemont 12. The rink’s season kicks off on Nov. 21, when Rosemont’s mayor flips the switch on 80,000 holiday lights during the family-friendly event. Also part of the festivities are visits with Santa and Mrs. Claus, horse-drawn sleigh rides and carolers. Parkway Bank Park is accessible via the Blue Line; parking is free with validation.
Gallagher Ice Rink
The Gallagher Ice Rink returns this season to Wrigleyville.
Provided
3635 N. Clark St.; 773-388-8260
Admission $8, skate rental $16
Nov. 20-Dec. 31
The Gallagher Ice Rink returns this season when Wrigleyville turns into Winterland. Before or after you take to the ice, shop for gifts at Christkindlmarket Wrigleyville, visit Santa’s Workshop and make your own wreath. Celebrate the holiday season during the annual Tree Lighting Ceremony Dec. 4, featuring performances from a local choir and other entertainers. Residents who live in ZIP codes 60613, 60614, 60640 and 60657 can pay reduced admission ($4 and $8 for skate rental) on Neighbor Discount Nights Mondays and Tuesdays.
Maggie Daley Park Ice Skating Ribbon
Surrounded by pine trees with views of the city’s skyscrapers, the quarter-mile, curved Ribbon forms a long trail with gentle inclines and dips.
Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times file
337 E. Randolph St.; 312-552-3000
$5 admission with own skates; $17 weekday skate rentals, $19 walk-in (Friday-Sunday and holiday rates are $21 skate rentals online, $23 walk-in)
Nov. 13-March 7, 2027
Surrounded by pine trees with views of the city’s skyscrapers, the quarter-mile, curved Ribbon forms a long trail with gentle inclines and dips. With a capacity for more than 700 skaters, the Ribbon seems to be the spot for couples so brace yourself for hand-holding pairs who must be navigated around. The site offers skate rentals, storage lockers and skate aids for children. Warm up with coffee, hot cocoa and tea from the Rink Cafe or satisfy your hunger with hot dogs, soups and burgers from Downtown Deli. The deli also sells S’mores kits, which you can roast at a nearby fire pit. Reservations for public skating at the Ribbon are highly recommended, and walk-up tickets aren’t guaranteed if a session is full.
McCormick Tribune Ice Rink in Millennium Park
McCormick Tribune Ice Rink in Millennium Park opens for the season Nov. 20.
Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times file
1 N. Michigan Ave.; 312-285-2361
Admission is free; $18 skate rentals Monday through Thursday and $22 Friday through Sunday and holidays (visitors bringing their own skates can skate free Monday through Thursday)
Nov. 20-Jan. 31, 2027; subject to weather
If you’re looking for a rink with a holiday rom-com vibe, look no further than the 16,000-square-foot oval at Millennium Park with its Christmas tree and views of the Bean. Don’t worry if you can’t skate like Olympic champ Alysa Liu; free ice-skating lessons are available for skaters of any age at three levels, including beginners. Lessons take place from 9-10 a.m. Saturdays and Sundays (weather permitting). Bonus: Skates are free for the lessons. Registrations are limited to 20 participants per class level. Preregistration online for public skates is strongly encouraged; sign-ups will open the Monday prior to each weekend. Walk-ups will be accepted if there are no-shows. Thursday, November 12, 2026 - WBEZ Chicago
The Rundown | Chicago News Podcast
Thursday, November 12, 2026
Nineteen of twenty Chicago School Board races on the ballot last Tuesday have now been called. The Abraham Lincoln Presidential Museum in Springfield has acquired a business ledger that offers a window into Lincoln’s early days as a lawyer. Chicago Blackhawks General Manager Kyle Davidson is speaking publicly about the team’s lackluster start. Plus, the proposed funding for Chicago’s 2027 arts budget is falling flat. Mayor Brandon Johnson’s plan pitches a less than 1% increase from last year. Advocates are calling the budget disappointing and say it pales in comparison to other major cities.

Climate scientists are anticipating that a record-breaking El Niño weather pattern will form this winter with global implications. A new clinic is welcoming its first furry patients in Chicago’s Chatham neighborhood. The Chicago Blackhawks have lost six straight games and capped off a brutal road trip on Saturday with a 9-2 loss to the Carolina Hurricanes. Plus, baked goods are having a moment in Chicago. Among the most popular baked bites – the humble croissant. We visited Floriole in Lincoln Park to investigate how to eat one.

Monday, November 9, 2026
Illinois U.S. Representative Delia Ramirez says she wants to see oversight into the Trump administration’s deportation campaigns following the midterm election results. South suburban Orland Hills has a new permanent drivers services facility. A record shop in Beverly on Chicago’s South Side celebrated its reopening Plus, new analysis by WBEZ finds the University of Chicago, like many universities, rarely expels students who are found responsible for sexual assault. That means most perpetrators of sexual violence are allowed to graduate and receive a UChicago diploma. Researchers and advocates say their presence on campus makes it even harder for survivors to stay in school and finish. UChicago students are calling for tougher discipline following two recent reports of assault tied to the Hyde Park campus.

More than two dozen Democratic Illinois State Representatives want to replace Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch. A dozen Chicago restaurants made a new list from reservation booking site OpenTable of the top 100 restaurants in the country. Four White Sox players are finalists for this year’s Silver Slugger Award. Plus, Chicago now has its own brewery for Korea’s oldest alcoholic drink. Makgeolli is a rice wine that has been around for centuries, and it’s now growing in popularity in the U.S.
